content: Mobile health, commonly referred to as mHealth, is a subset of eHealth. The Global Observatory for eHealth (GOe) defines mHealth as the practice of medicine and public health supported by mobile devices, including mobile phones, patient monitoring devices, personal digital assistants (PDAs), and other wireless devices. mHealth leverages the basic functionalities of mobile phones, such as voice communication and short messaging service (SMS), as well as more advanced features like general packet radio service (GPRS), thirdand fourth-generation mobile telecommunications (3G and 4G systems), global positioning system (GPS), and Bluetooth technology. In the current era, where technology is deeply integrated into all aspects of life, it is reasonable to anticipate that mHealth will become a fundamental component of healthcare delivery. Observational studies have shown that most patients, even those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, own smartphones and express interest in using them to enhance their health. However, there are potential limitations, such as the accuracy of smartphone accelerometers in estimating energy expenditure and concerns about the usability and functionality of health-related applications. Gamification may improve the effectiveness of these applications. Complex clinical trials are being initiated to evaluate the effectiveness of mHealth interventions. Regarding medication adherence, mobile phone strategies have shown mixed results. For example, in the context of primary prevention of cardiovascular disease, mobile phone-based interventions have demonstrated low-quality evidence for improving medication compliance. However, a meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials involving patients with chronic diseases found that text messaging approximately doubles the odds of medication adherence. More recent trials have confirmed these benefits. In terms of physical activity, a 2018 proof-of-concept randomized controlled trial demonstrated that fitness trackers could promote behavioral changes, such as goal setting and social support, within the framework of social cognitive therapy. These changes were further enhanced by counseling with motivational interviewing. These findings align with prior systematic reviews of overweight individuals. mHealth has the potential to increase patient engagement. A prospective randomized controlled trial found that participants using a mobile application to track their chronic disease experienced improved health self-management compared to those who did not use such an application. However, there is currently insufficient evidence to conclude that mobile phone messaging interventions significantly improve health outcomes. They may, however, enhance a patient’s ability to self-manage their disease. A 2012 Cochrane Review of four studies on mobile phone messaging interventions for managing chronic diseases (diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and asthma) found no significant differences in glycemic control, blood pressure control, or lung function values (FVC/FEV1) between intervention and control groups. However, the asthma-focused study did report a significant improvement in pooled asthma symptom scores favoring the text messaging intervention. All four studies reviewed showed evidence of improved disease self-monitoring or better medication adherence with mobile phone messaging interventions. For coronary artery disease, a randomized controlled trial demonstrated a reduction in risk factors associated with mHealth use. Conversely, a trial on hypertension found no benefit. Meta-analyses published in 2019, including reviews of randomized trials and other study designs, found that mHealth interventions augmented by healthcare providers or study personnel were beneficial. Additionally, a trial not included in these reviews reported a greater decline in hemoglobin A1c levels, and a more recent trial also found reductions in HbA1c. Regarding physical activity, systematic reviews from 2016 and 2020 concluded that mHealth interventions increase physical activity. Text messaging may provide short-term improvements, and performance feedback from mobile devices about progress toward goals can enhance motivation, as supported by trials and reviews. In the context of weight loss and obesity, a systematic review for the Community Guide found that electronic activity monitors increase physical activity. However, a 2014 randomized controlled trial evaluating the efficacy of the MyFitnessPal application for weight loss in a primary care setting found no significant difference in weight loss compared to usual care. Notably, most participants stopped using the application after the first month of the study. A second randomized controlled trial also yielded negative results. In contrast, a 2013 pilot randomized controlled trial found that a smartphone app could improve adherence and total weight loss after six months compared to a website monitoring group. In this study, 128 overweight individuals were randomized to receive a weight management intervention delivered via smartphone app, website, or paper diary. The smartphone app intervention, My Meal Mate (MMM), was developed using an evidence-based behavioral approach. Trial retention was highest in the smartphone group (93%) compared to the website group (55%) and the paper diary group (53%) at six months. Adherence was also higher in the smartphone group, with a mean of 92 days compared to 35 days in the website group and 29 days in the paper diary group. In terms of diagnostic assistance, preliminary research suggests that smartphone cameras may be capable of using photoplethysmography to detect atrial fibrillation.
